answer: I'd like to talk about something small that I keep in a drawer beside my bed. An object with deep sentimental value to me is an old wristwatch that belonged to my grandfather. He wore it for decades, and a few years ago, when the small dial became hard for him to read, he took it off his wrist and gave it to me. He lives in our ancestral village not far from Sirajganj, and I still remember him pressing it into my hand during one of our visits and telling me to look after it better than he had. So I've had it for about four years now. The watch itself is fairly worn and no longer even keeps perfect time, yet I would not trade it for anything. The leather strap is cracked and the glass has a tiny scratch across it, but I've deliberately never had it polished. What makes it so [[precious]] is the memories it carries; I remember him glancing at it constantly throughout my childhood. Holding it now brings back a flood of warm, [[nostalgic]] feelings. It is a [[tangible connection]] to a man I love and admire deeply. He is in his eighties now but still remarkably sharp, and he always asks whether I'm taking care of it. I keep it safely stored and only take it out occasionally, almost like a [[relic]]. Honestly, its emotional worth is completely disconnected from its monetary value. I think objects like this become [[irreplaceable]] precisely because of the people and memories attached to them. One day I hope to pass it on to my own children, along with the stories of the wonderful man who gave it to me.

followUps.q: Do you ever wear the watch?
followUps.answer: Only occasionally, usually when I visit my grandfather. He always notices straight away and smiles, which makes it feel like a small, shared ritual between the two of us.

followUps.q: Do you think young people value old things as much as older people do?
followUps.answer: Perhaps not always. Many young people prefer new things, but I think we [[come to appreciate]] old objects later in life, once we understand the memories and stories behind them.
